title.en: Climate-Resilient Taiwan – Adapting to Extreme Weather

narrative_brief:
🌍 Mission: SDG 13 – The Climate Speech Puzzle
任務：SDG 13——氣候演說大拼圖

Can you save the planet in 6 minutes and 40 seconds? The world is heating up, and your script is a mess! Before you can deliver your epic Pecha Kucha talk, you need to fix the "Information Meltdown."
你能用 6 分 40 秒拯救地球嗎？ 世界正在升溫，而你的講稿卻亂成一團！在你發表超強的 Pecha Kucha 演說之前，你需要先修復這場「資訊大熔爐」。

Step 1: Know Your Battle Plan (熟悉你的作戰計畫)
每個英雄都需要地圖。要打敗氣候危機，你的演說必須經過這 6 個關卡：
Part 1 The Hook (引言): Wake them up! (喚醒聽眾！)
Part 2 The Bad News (問題指認): Why is the Earth sweaty? (為什麼地球在流汗？)
Part 3 The "Good Job" Part (成果進展): Taiwan’s small wins. (台灣的小小勝利。)
Part 4 The Nerd Power (解決方案): STEM to the rescue! (科技救地球！)
Part 5 The Reality Check (挑戰與衝擊): It’s not that easy... (沒那麼簡單……)
Part 6 The Mic Drop (結語與行動): Tell them what to do! (震撼結尾，呼籲行動！)

Step 2: The 20-Second Scramble (20 秒限時大亂鬥)
根據關鍵字，猜猜這張投影片屬於哪個「關卡」。
將碎片按正確順序排列，重建這場 6 分 40 秒的傑作。

Step 3: Level Up Your Brain (腦力大升級)
拼圖完成後，先別急著走！問問自己：
✔ Why this piece? (為什麼是這片？) 是什麼關鍵字告訴你它屬於那裡？
✔ The Flow (流暢度): 講者如何從「嚴肅的氣候變化議題」轉向「有意義的資訊分享與行動」而不讓聽眾分心？

A2.text: Every spring we wait for the rain, and nothing comes. Then the typhoons arrive and drop a whole year of water in two days. Today, let's watch our island cope.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Is our weather getting strange? We have no rain for months, and then scary typhoons arrive. The climate is changing fast. Today, let’s see how our island can adapt together.

B1.text: Adaptation is the half of climate action nobody puts on a poster. Yet here the rain disappears for months, and then one storm returns an entire year of it in two days.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Have you noticed that our weather is acting strange lately? We go from months of no rain straight into scary typhoons. The climate is changing fast. Today, we will explore how our island can adapt to this new, wild weather reality.

B2.text: Something in our water cycle has broken. The rain withholds itself for months, then a single system returns an entire year of it within forty-eight hours, and adaptation is what we do about that.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Have you observed the erratic behavior of our weather patterns recently? We are increasingly oscillating between prolonged months of severe drought and catastrophic typhoons. This climate volatility is accelerating rapidly. Today, we will examine how our island can effectively adapt to this harsh, unpredictable weather reality.

A2.text: SDG 13 is Climate Action. Most people think it only means less carbon gas. It also means cities that survive a disaster, and water that still runs.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: SDG 13 means Climate Action. It is not just about cutting carbon. It also tells us to build strong, safe cities that can survive big natural disasters and protect our lives.

B1.text: Everyone hears Climate Action and thinks of cutting carbon. Read the goal properly and half of it is about survival: drains that cope, homes that stand, and a supply that holds.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: SDG 13 demands urgent action to fight climate change. But it is not just about stopping carbon emissions. It also tells us to build strong cities that can survive natural disasters. We must learn to protect our water, homes, and lives.

B2.text: The goal is usually reduced to carbon accounting, yet mitigation covers barely half of what the text actually demands. The remainder is resilience: drainage that copes, buildings that survive, and a municipal supply that never fails.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: SDG 13 explicitly mandates urgent global intervention against climate change. Crucially, this encompasses more than just mitigation through carbon reduction. It also dictates that we enhance disaster resilience across our urban environments, implementing defensive strategies to protect our water supplies, local infrastructure, and human lives.

A2.text: Taiwan gets plenty of rain. But we are a water-poor island, because our mountains are steep. The rain runs into the sea before we can catch it.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Taiwan gets much rain, but we are a 'water-poor island'. Our high mountains push rainwater straight into the sea. Keeping water where we need it is a big challenge for us.

B1.text: We are officially a water-poor island, which sounds absurd in a place this wet. The mountains are simply too steep, so the rain reaches the sea long before it reaches a reservoir.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Taiwan gets a lot of rain, but we are actually an officially 'water-poor' island. Our high mountains push rain straight into the ocean. Because of this geographic challenge, keeping water where we need it is a matter of survival for us.

B2.text: Taiwan is formally classified as water-poor, a description that sounds absurd in a subtropical climate. The explanation is topographical: precipitation reaches the ocean within hours of landing, long before any catchment can retain it.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Despite receiving substantial annual rainfall, Taiwan is paradoxically designated as a water-poor island. Our steep mountainous topography causes precipitation to drain rapidly into the ocean. Due to this geographic vulnerability, capturing and retaining freshwater resources has become an absolute matter of survival for our nation.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

A2.text: Typhoons now come less often, but they hit harder. In our worst drought, the reservoirs went dry. Rice fields cracked open, and the chip factories nearly stopped.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Data shows that our typhoons are fewer but stronger. Recently, we faced terrible droughts. Our reservoirs dried up completely, and our famous chip factories almost ran out of water.

B1.text: Fewer typhoons sounds like good news until you remember that they refill our reservoirs. During the last great drought the storage simply ran out, rice fields cracked open, and the chip plants came close to stopping.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Climate data shows a dangerous trend: Taiwan’s typhoons are decreasing, but becoming much stronger. In recent years, we faced historical droughts where reservoirs completely dried up. Without rain, our rice fields cracked, and our semiconductor factories almost ran out of water.

B2.text: Typhoons appear to be arriving less frequently while intensifying, and fewer storms means fewer refills. During the last severe drought reservoir storage was effectively exhausted, paddy fields fractured, and semiconductor fabrication came remarkably close to halting.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Meteorological trends reveal a disturbing pattern: typhoons hitting Taiwan are decreasing in frequency but escalating in intensity. Consequently, we have faced unprecedented droughts where vital reservoirs dried up completely, threatening agricultural yields and nearly paralyzing the water-dependent semiconductor manufacturing sector.

A2.text: Then the opposite happens. A year of rain can fall in two days. Our old drains cannot take it, so the streets turn into brown rivers.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: The other problem is extreme rainfall. Sometimes, a year of rain falls in just two days! Our old city drains cannot handle this water, and streets become dangerous rivers.

B1.text: Then the island floods. A single storm can deliver a year's rainfall in two days, and drains laid for a calmer century give up, turning shopping streets into brown rivers.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: The other side of the problem is extreme rainfall. When storms hit, a year's worth of rain can fall in just two days. Our old city drains cannot handle this sudden water. Streets turn into dangerous rivers, causing massive economic damage.

B2.text: The opposite failure is equally expensive. When a storm stalls over the island, a year of precipitation can arrive within forty-eight hours, overwhelming drainage designed for a gentler century and converting commercial streets into rivers.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Conversely, we simultaneously face the menace of extreme rainfall. During severe storms, a year's worth of precipitation frequently floods urban centers within forty-eight hours. Our outdated drainage infrastructure simply cannot handle this volume, turning municipal streets into hazardous rivers and causing massive economic devastation.

A2.text: So here are the hard questions. Can our old pipes survive this new weather? And can we save the flood water for the dry months?
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: We must ask some tough questions. Can our cities survive these fast climate changes? How can we store flood water for dry days? Our young scientists must find answers now.

B1.text: Two questions follow, and neither has a comfortable answer. Can pipes designed for the last climate survive this one? And can we hold floodwater long enough to drink it in the dry season?
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: This leaves us with serious questions. Can our infrastructure survive these climate swings? How can we store water safely during floods to use during severe droughts? These are the dangerous puzzles that our young scientists must solve right now.

B2.text: Two engineering questions follow, and neither has a comfortable answer. Can public works designed for a previous climate withstand the current one? And can floodwater be intercepted and stored rather than discharged straight into the sea?
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: These alarming shifts force us to confront critical inquiries. Can our existing public works withstand such intense climate fluctuations? How do we safely intercept floodwaters to supplement our reserves during dry periods? These are the complex puzzles our young researchers must solve immediately.

A2.text: Taiwan is already working on this. We now have the Forward-looking Water Grid. It joins the pipes of many cities, so Tainan can send spare water to Kaohsiung.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Taiwan is acting. The government built a large Smart Water Grid. We connected water pipes between different cities. Now, we can pump backup water to dry places easily.

B1.text: Taiwan has not been standing still. The Forward-looking Water Grid has linked the pipelines of neighbouring cities, so when Kaohsiung runs short, spare supply can be pumped across from Tainan instead.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Fortunately, Taiwan has not been standing still. The government built an impressive 'Forward-looking Water Grid.' We connected pipelines between different cities. Now, if Kaohsiung is dry, we can safely pump backup water from Tainan. It is a great network.

B2.text: The official response has been infrastructural. Under the Forward-looking Water Grid, municipal pipelines have been interconnected, allowing surplus volume to be transferred from Tainan toward Kaohsiung whenever one reservoir falls below its operating reserve.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Fortunately, Taiwan is proactively responding. The government has engineered an advanced, integrated Smart Water Grid, linking distribution pipelines across different municipalities. This nationwide network allows authorities to seamlessly divert backup water from resilient zones to drought-stricken regions, stabilizing our collective supply.

A2.text: Taipei and Taichung want to be sponge cities. New pavements let the rain soak through. Parks are built low, so a storm can fill them first.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Cities like Taipei are becoming 'Sponge Cities'. We use special roads that drink rainwater. Also, our beautiful parks can hold flood water safely underground during big storms.

B1.text: Taipei and Taichung are being rebuilt as sponge cities. Solid concrete is giving way to pavement that lets rain through, and parks are sunk below the road so that a storm fills them first.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Major cities like Taipei and Taichung are turning into 'Sponge Cities.' We are replacing regular concrete roads with permeable pavement that drinks water. Parks are designed to act as giant temporary lakes during floods, holding rainwater safely underground.

B2.text: Taipei and Taichung are being retrofitted as sponge cities. Impermeable concrete is gradually replaced by porous surfacing, while parks are engineered as retention basins, deliberately sunk so a deluge collects there rather than in the surrounding streets.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Metropolitan areas like Taipei are progressively transforming into Sponge Cities. Engineers are replacing standard impermeable concrete with advanced permeable pavements. Furthermore, urban parks are strategically designed to serve as major eco-retention basins during deluges, temporarily storing excess stormwater safely underground.

A2.text: Our farmers are changing too. A computer gives each rice plant the exact water it needs, drop by drop. This saves millions of tons a year.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Taiwanese farmers are using smart technology to save water. Computer systems give rice plants the exact water they need through 'drip irrigation'. This saves millions of tons of water.

B1.text: Farming has changed as well. Computer-controlled drip irrigation gives a rice plant exactly the water it needs and nothing more, which saves millions of tons across the island every season.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Taiwanese farmers are also adapting beautifully. They are using smart technology to save water in agriculture. By using computerized 'drip irrigation,' they give rice plants the exact amount of water needed. This local progress saves millions of tons of water.

B2.text: Agriculture has adapted comparably. Computerised drip irrigation delivers precisely the volume a crop requires, eliminating the surplus that older methods wasted, and conserving millions of tons of freshwater annually across the island.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Furthermore, Taiwanese agriculture is adapting through smart technology integration. Farmers are utilizing automated irrigation systems to optimize water efficiency. By transitioning to computerized drip irrigation protocols, they deliver the exact volume required by crops, successfully conserving millions of tons of vital water annually.

stages.source_description: Solutions and STEM Integration (解決方案與 STEM 整合)

A2.text: How does STEM help? Engineers put small sensors inside the water pipes. The data goes to a computer, which finds a hidden leak in minutes.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: How does STEM help? Engineers put IoT sensors inside water pipes. These sensors send data to AI systems to find underground leaks instantly. This stops water waste.

B1.text: This is where STEM earns its place. Engineers have fitted sensors inside the mains, and the data they stream lets a computer locate a buried leak in minutes rather than months.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: How does STEM save the day? Taiwan engineers use IoT sensors inside water pipes. These sensors send real-time data to AI systems. The computers can detect hidden underground leaks instantly. This technology prevents precious clean water from wasting away into the soil.

B2.text: Here the engineering becomes genuinely elegant. Sensors embedded in the mains stream continuous flow data to an analytical system that identifies a buried leak within minutes, long before the loss becomes visible at the surface.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: How can STEM innovation safeguard our resources? Engineers are embedding advanced IoT sensors directly into municipal water lines. These devices stream real-time flow data to centralized AI diagnostics, enabling utility teams to pinpoint and repair subterranean leaks instantly before precious water vanishes.

A2.text: We also make new water. Factories clean their used water until it is pure again. On the coast, new plants take the salt out of sea water.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Another great STEM tool is water recycling. Factories clean used water until it is pure again. Taiwan also builds desalination plants to turn ocean water into safe drinking water.

B1.text: We are also manufacturing water. Industrial wastewater is purified until it can go straight back into the production line, and plants on the coast can pull the salt out of seawater in an emergency.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Another brilliant STEM solution is advanced water recycling. High-tech water plants now clean industrial wastewater until it is perfectly pure again. Taiwan is also building solar-powered desalination plants to turn ocean water into safe drinking water during emergencies.

B2.text: Water is increasingly manufactured rather than merely collected. Industrial effluent is reclaimed to a purity that permits reuse, and coastal desalination offers an emergency buffer, although extracting salt from seawater consumes a considerable amount of electricity.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Industrial sectors are embracing recycling breakthroughs. Modern purification facilities process manufacturing wastewater until it achieves total purity for reuse. Simultaneously, Taiwan is constructing solar-powered desalination plants along coastal areas, providing an alternative buffer to convert seawater into potable resources during emergencies.

A2.text: Up in the mountains, we fight landslides too. Instead of tall cement walls, we use rocks and local plants. They hold the soil and keep our rivers clean.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: In our mountains, scientists use 'Eco-Engineering' to stop landslides. They use natural rocks and plants instead of cement walls. This keeps our rivers clean and safe.

B1.text: In the mountains the same thinking applies to landslides. Rather than pouring another concrete wall, engineers anchor the slope with rock and local planting, which keeps the mud out of our reservoirs.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: In our mountains, scientists use 'Eco-Engineering' to prevent landslides. Instead of building ugly cement walls, they use natural rocks and local plants to hold the soil. This protects our river basins and keeps our reservoirs clean from muddy pollution.

B2.text: The same philosophy governs our unstable highlands. Rather than pouring further concrete, engineers stabilise slopes with rock structures and indigenous planting, an approach that protects the river basin and prevents sediment from silting up reservoirs downstream.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: In vulnerable highlands, geologists implement Eco-Engineering to mitigate landslide risks. Rather than deploying disruptive concrete retaining walls, they utilize indigenous vegetation and natural rock barriers to reinforce slopes. This ecological approach stabilizes river basins and prevents mudslides from clogging downstream reservoirs.

stages.source_description: Implications and Future Challenges (影響與未來挑戰)

A2.text: But none of this is cheap. New water plants and big pipes cost billions of dollars. So who pays for it? We must be fair to ordinary families.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: However, climate defense is very expensive. Building new water plants costs billions of dollars. We must debate a hard topic: how do we pay for this without hurting regular citizens?

B1.text: None of this is cheap, and the bill has to land somewhere. Recycling plants and deep pipelines cost billions of dollars, so the honest question is how we pay without squeezing ordinary households.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: However, protecting our island is incredibly expensive. Building recycled water plants and giant underground pipes costs billions of dollars. We must debate a difficult topic: how do we pay for climate defense without raising taxes too much for regular citizens?

B2.text: Nothing here is inexpensive, and the invoice eventually arrives somewhere. Reclamation facilities and deep tunnels absorb billions of dollars of capital, so the genuine political question is how such defences are financed without penalising ordinary households.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Nevertheless, fortifying our nation against climate impacts introduces severe financial friction. Constructing advanced recycling facilities requires immense capital investments. We must resolve a complex fiscal debate: how can we fund these critical defenses equitably without placing a disproportionate tax burden on average citizens?

A2.text: There is also a fair-share problem. The rich tech cities get the new water systems first. But small farm villages go dry first, and that is not right.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: We also face a challenge with 'Climate Justice'. Rich tech cities get smart water tools fast, but small farming villages suffer first during droughts. We must protect everyone equally.

B1.text: There is a fairness problem hidden inside all of this. The wealthy technology cities receive the new systems first, while farming villages are the first to have their water cut during a drought.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: We also face a challenge with 'Climate Justice.' Big high-tech cities get advanced water infrastructure quickly. But small farming villages often suffer first during droughts. We must ensure that our climate solutions protect rural communities equally, leaving no one behind.

B2.text: A distributional problem is embedded in every one of these projects. Affluent technology corridors receive upgraded systems first, whereas agricultural communities are typically the earliest to have their allocation restricted once a drought is declared.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: We must also address issues regarding Climate Justice. While wealthy high-tech metropolises receive sophisticated infrastructure updates rapidly, vulnerable agricultural communities are often the first to suffer during seasonal droughts. Our adaptive policies must protect rural populations equally, ensuring equitable resource distribution.

A2.text: Other islands have the same trouble, and our answers could help them. But Taiwan cannot speak at the big climate meetings. We must share in other ways.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Taiwan’s technology can help the world. But international politics makes it hard for Taiwan to join global climate meetings. We need creative ways to share our green knowledge.

B1.text: Other island nations face exactly these problems, and what we have learned could genuinely help them. Politics keeps Taiwan out of the major climate summits, so the knowledge has to travel by other routes.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Taiwan’s extreme weather adaptation can help the world. Many island nations face the exact same sea-level threats. However, international political issues make it hard for Taiwan to join global climate summits. We need to find creative ways to share our technology.

B2.text: Other island states confront an identical set of pressures, and our accumulated experience would transfer directly. Political exclusion keeps Taiwan outside the major climate summits, which means this knowledge has to circulate through unofficial channels.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Taiwan’s adaptation breakthroughs offer invaluable blueprints for the international community, particularly other island nations threatened by rising sea levels. However, complex international politics frequently obstruct Taiwan from participating in global climate summits. We must devise alternative diplomatic channels to share our technological insights.

A2.text: One more job is ours. We must check that these new systems still work, and are not just for show. Ask for the data every year.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: Finally, we must watch these projects closely. Are these green tools working properly, or were they just built for show? As citizens, we need honesty and data transparency.

B1.text: Finally, somebody has to check the work. A sponge park that nobody maintains is only landscaping, so citizens should be asking for the inspection data on our dams and drains every year.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: Finally, we must monitor these projects closely. Are these green systems being maintained properly, or were they just built for show? As citizens, we must check the safety data of our dams and cities. Continuous honesty is required to survive 2050.

B2.text: Finally, all of this demands sustained public scrutiny. An unmaintained retention basin is merely expensive landscaping, so citizens should insist on published inspection data, because this infrastructure has to be functioning in 2050.
B2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B2.workbook_text: Finally, rigorous public oversight is essential. We must continuously evaluate if these ecological adaptations are fully functional over time, or simply constructed for public relations. Citizens must demand complete data transparency regarding infrastructure structural health to ensure long-term climate survivability.

stages.source_description: Conclusion and Call to Action (結論與行動號召)

A2.text: So what have we learned? Taiwan is learning to live with wild weather. Sponge cities, smart pipes and good engineering are making a weak island strong.
A2.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
A2.workbook_text: To sum up, Taiwan is learning to live with extreme weather. Through sponge cities and STEM engineering, we are turning our vulnerable island into a resilient leader. We are ready.

B1.text: So where does that leave us? Sponge cities, a connected grid and a great deal of engineering are turning a vulnerable island into a prepared one. We cannot stop the storms, but we can meet them.
B1.authored_by: Claude (English teacher role), authored against the v2 quality gate
B1.workbook_text: To sum up, Taiwan is learning to live with extreme weather. Through sponge cities, smart water grids, and STEM engineering, we are turning a vulnerable island into a resilient leader. We cannot stop the storms, but we can be ready.

B1.workbook_text: Why does this matter to you? Because climate adaptation needs new ideas. You can study earth science, engineering, or coding to build better disaster systems. At home, you can practice water conservation. Every single saved drop makes our island stronger.

A2.text: Please do not feel helpless. People are clever and nature is strong. Together they can protect this island and give our children a safe home.

B1.text: None of this should leave you feeling powerless. Human ingenuity and natural systems can work together rather than against each other, and Taiwan has both the skill and the nerve to prove it.

B2.workbook_text: Do not let the scale of climate change paralyze your potential. Human creativity and technological innovation can successfully harmonize with natural systems.
